comparison: Two layouts of the same generated fwp program: embedded heap cancellation state versus a borrowed buffer in the live task entry frame. No C/Rust baseline.
workload: tests/fixtures/task_channel_ownership.fwp; fixed strings, 65 string-producing task-map inputs, two 64-round channel construction loops, successful/repeated awaits, early and suspended cancellation, nested queues, state and errors. Output matches raw interpretation and the stored fixture.
scope: Managed allocation requests, unrounded requested bytes, effective retains and sampled peak/final managed charge after constant initialization through normal teardown. Small allocations use rounded size classes; large allocations charge requested bytes. Both measured layouts disable collection, retain normal freeing and have the same hooks. Total process memory and elapsed time are not measured.
compilation: fwp O1 emits each memory-mode source once. Native C O0/O2 use the named host compiler, GNU C11, disabled floating contraction and explicit FWP_LTO=0. Compiler identity, flags and runtime libraries are recorded per host.
correctness: Eight measured binaries plus two normal lifetime-check binaries and four deliberate setup/clear omissions per native host. Tracing verification uses collection stress and reuse poisoning; ARC excludes tracing. All actual binaries and generated C hashes were checked, with entry disassembly and symbols. Focused suites also run task handles, scopes, timers, library unload, static memory and affected compiler/numerical cancellation tests.
limits: Smaller heap records still require saved bytes in child stacks and leave less usable stack space. Entry-frame sizes are static prologue reservations, not whole-stack peaks. Allocation requests and retains remain. No speed, process-memory, cache or zero-ARC claim. Focused acceptance does not replace final-head production CI.
reproduction: Dispatch numerics.yml at the source tag with suite=task-cancellation and native_runner=all, then suite=wasm-hosts and native_runner=all. Native artifacts contain C, executables, outputs/statuses, symbols, disassembly, sections, compiler identities and machine metadata. WASI artifacts contain executed modules and diagnostic controls.
